noteBlocks.md:
A pulse that comes back has been on **two journeys**: out to whatever reflected it, and back again. The timer starts when the pulse leaves and stops when the echo arrives, so the time you are given always covers **both**.
That is the whole idea of this topic. Speed × time gives the **total** distance the pulse covered, and the distance you actually want is **half** of it.

noteBlocks.explain: Both journeys — which is why the total has to be halved before it becomes a depth.

noteBlocks.title: The echo rule, and its two directions
noteBlocks.md:
**distance to the reflector = (speed × time) ÷ 2**
Going the other way, from a known distance to a speed: **speed = (2 × distance) ÷ time**. Whichever direction you work in, the factor of two appears exactly once, and neither form is printed anywhere in the paper.

A ship's sonar pulse returns 0.12 s after it was sent. Sound travels through sea water at 1500 m/s.
**Step 1** — total distance $= 1500 \times 0.12 = 180$ m.
**Step 2** — that covers down **and** back, so halve it.
**Step 3** — depth $= 180 \div 2 = 90$ m.
The depth must always come out smaller than the total, never larger.

noteBlocks.prompt: A shout echoes back from a cliff 0.5 s later, and sound travels at 340 m/s in air. How far away is the cliff, in m?
noteBlocks.explain: $(340 \times 0.5) \div 2 = 85$ m. The sound covered 170 m altogether, and the cliff is half that away.

noteBlocks.title: Why the journey is halved
noteBlocks.md: The pulse travels out to whatever reflects it and back again, so the time you measure covers the depth twice. Halving is what turns a there-and-back measurement into a one-way distance, and a question that hands you the distance instead turns that factor of two the other way round.

**Ultrasound** is sound with a frequency greater than **20 000 Hz** — too high for a human ear, but still sound, so still **longitudinal** and still needing particles to travel through.
The specification gives it exactly two uses. In **medicine**, measuring the **head diameter of a foetus**. In **industry**, **detecting defects in metals**.

noteBlocks.md:
Inside a steel casting the same rule does the work. A pulse sent in from the surface reflects at **every boundary** it meets: first from a crack, later from the far face. An engineer reads the **arrival times** and turns each one into a depth with the same halving.
An **earlier echo means a shorter distance**, which is how a flaw nobody can see is found and measured.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two echoes come back from one pulse sent into a steel block. What does the earlier one tell the engineer?
options: something is reflecting the pulse closer to the surface
the block is made of two different metals
the pulse is travelling faster near the surface
noteBlocks.answer: something is reflecting the pulse closer to the surface
noteBlocks.explain: Earlier means nearer. The speed is the same throughout the block, so a shorter time can only mean a shorter journey.

noteBlocks.text: 5. Sonar, radar, and the other direction

noteBlocks.md:
Two systems, one principle, different waves. **Sonar** sends **pulses of sound** through water, to find the seabed, shoals of fish or wrecks. **Radar** sends **electromagnetic waves** through air, to find **aircraft and ships**.
And the factor of two runs backwards too: given a known distance and a there-and-back time, **double the distance first**, then divide by the time to get a speed.

noteBlocks.prompt: A clap echoes back from a wall 34 m away, 0.2 s later. What is the speed of sound, in m/s?
noteBlocks.explain: The sound covered $2 \times 34 = 68$ m in 0.2 s, so the speed is $68 \div 0.2 = 340$ m/s.

items.stem: Before we start, from P1: rearranged to give a distance, what does speed = distance ÷ time become?

options.feedback: That rearrangement is the engine of every echo calculation.
Dividing by the time would make a long journey come out short. Multiply.
That is upside down. Distance = speed × time.

items.stem: From the last topic: sound is which kind of wave?

options.feedback: Longitudinal, and so is ultrasound, which is only sound too high to hear.
Water waves and electromagnetic waves are transverse. Sound is longitudinal — the waves topic covers this first.

items.stem: How many milliseconds are there in one second?

options.feedback: 1000. Echo times often arrive in milliseconds and have to be converted before substituting.
Milli means a thousandth, so there are 1000 milliseconds in a second.
60 is seconds in a minute. Milli means a thousandth.

options.text: sound with a frequency above 20 000 Hz
options.feedback: That is the specification's wording, and the number is what carries the mark.
Those are two different things. Ultraviolet is electromagnetic; ultrasound is sound. Examiners have reported the two words being swapped.

options.text: a transverse wave that can travel through a vacuum
options.feedback: Ultrasound is sound, so it is longitudinal and it needs particles to travel through. Only electromagnetic waves cross a vacuum.

items.stem: A sonar pulse returns from the seabed 0.2 s after it was sent. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in the water. How deep is the water?

options.feedback: (1500 × 0.2) ÷ 2. The pulse covers the depth twice, so halve the total.
That is the total path of the pulse, down and back. The seabed is half as deep.
That halves twice. Halve the total distance once, and only once.
Speed divided by time is not a distance. Multiply the speed by the time, then halve.

items.stem: Why is the time halved in an echo calculation?

options.text: because the pulse travels to the reflector and back, covering twice the distance
options.feedback: That is the whole reason, and it is what the scheme wants written down.

options.text: because the echo is only half as loud as the pulse that was sent out

parts.stem:
A fishing boat sends one sonar pulse straight down. The echo from the seabed arrives 0.1 s later. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water.
Calculate the depth of the water.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation line is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

hints: The pulse goes down to the seabed and back up to the boat.
parts.workedSolution: Using distance to the reflector = (speed × time) ÷ 2: the pulse covers 1500 × 0.1 = 150 m in total, so the water is 75 m deep.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the whole journey of the pulse. Halve it: the seabed is half as deep as the pulse's total path.

parts.stem:
The same pulse also produced an earlier echo, arriving 0.04 s after the pulse was sent. This echo came from a shoal of fish.
Calculate the depth of the shoal.
hints: Same rule, different time.
An earlier echo must come from something closer.
parts.workedSolution: The rule is unchanged: (1500 × 0.04) ÷ 2 = 30 m. The echo arrived earlier because the shoal is nearer the boat than the seabed is.

commonErrors.feedback: The halving is missing again. Every echo distance is halved, because every echo is a there-and-back journey.

parts.stem: Use your answers to parts (a) and (b) to work out how far the shoal is above the seabed.
hints: Both depths are measured from the surface.
parts.workedSolution: Both depths are measured down from the surface, so the gap is 75 − 30 = 45 m.

commonErrors.feedback: The two depths were added. Both are measured down from the same surface, so subtract to find the gap between them.

scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Tell the story in order: send, reflect, receive, time, calculate, halve.
The halving needs a reason, not just an instruction.
parts.workedSolution: The depth sounder sends a short pulse of sound downwards from the hull of the vessel. The pulse travels through the water, reflects from the seabed and returns as an echo, which a detector on the vessel picks up. An electronic timer measures the time between the pulse leaving and the echo arriving. The speed of sound in sea water is already known, so the total distance travelled by the pulse can be found from distance = speed × time. That total is the journey down to the seabed and back up again, which is twice the depth, so the depth of the water is half of it.

findTheMistake.stem:
Dara is asked: 'A sonar pulse sent from a boat returns 0.16 s after it was sent. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water. Calculate the depth of the water. [4]'

findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The equation line is incomplete. Speed × time gives the distance the pulse travelled altogether, and the pulse went down to the seabed and back up to the boat. The rule for an echo is distance to the reflector = (speed × time) ÷ 2, so the depth is 240 ÷ 2 = 120 m.

prompts.answer: The smaller one. Speed × time gives the whole there-and-back path, so the distance to the reflector is always half of it and can never be the larger value.
